title: Given a string, find the minimum number of characters you must insert anywhere to make it a palindrome. Explain how the Palindromic Subsequence pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Minimum Insertions to Form a Palindrome (Fewest Additions for Symmetry)
keyPoints: Minimum insertions equals string length minus the longest palindromic subsequence length.
Characters in the LPS already have symmetric partners; every character outside the LPS needs one mirror partner inserted.
The LPS recurrence: matching ends add 2 to the inner answer; mismatching ends take the max of dropping one end.
This value equals the minimum deletions to make a palindrome, because deleting and inserting are symmetric fixes.
Time and space complexity are both O(n squared) for the DP table.
Space can be reduced to O(n) with a rolling two-row array.

s1_definition.oneliner: Minimum insertions equal the string length minus the longest palindromic subsequence length.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Key insight** is that characters in the longest palindromic subsequence already have their mirror partners; only the remaining characters need mirrors inserted.
- **LPS computation** uses the range DP: matching ends add 2, mismatching ends take the max of dropping one end.
- **Insertions** equal `n - LPS`, one mirror per unmatched character.
- **Equals minimum deletions** because deleting an unmatched character and inserting its mirror are symmetric.
- **O(n squared) time and space** for the DP table.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India pads short reference codes into a symmetric canonical shape by adding the fewest characters so the code reads the same both ways. The fewest insertions equal the code length minus its longest symmetric core, because only the characters without a mirror partner need one inserted.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  String: "ABCDA" (n=5)

  LPS = "ADA" (length 3)
  Unmatched characters: B, C (2 characters)
  Each needs a mirror inserted.

  Original:  A  B  C  D  A
  LPS:       A        D  A    ← these stay
  Insert:       B' C'         ← mirrors for B and C

  Result:    A  B  C  D  C' B' A
             = "ABCDCBA" (palindrome)

  Min insertions = n - LPS = 5 - 3 = 2

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Insertions = Deletions = n - LPS    │
  │  Both fix the same unmatched chars   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Minimum Insertions to Form a Palindrome reduces to the Longest Palindromic Subsequence, just like the minimum deletions problem. Characters in the LPS already have their mirror partners and stay in place. Every character outside the LPS needs a mirror partner inserted, so the answer is `n - LPS`.

Rajesh at the National Bank of India uses this to pad short reference codes into a symmetric canonical shape for a fixed template. The LPS is computed with the standard range DP: matching ends add 2, mismatching ends take the max of dropping one end. The answer is read from the corner of the table.

The deep connection is that minimum insertions and minimum deletions give the same number for making a string palindrome. Deleting an unmatched character and inserting its mirror are two symmetric ways to fix the same asymmetry. Explaining this duality in an interview shows understanding of the pattern beyond mechanical DP construction.

The time and space are both O(n squared), reducible to O(n) space with a rolling array. A palindrome needs 0 insertions, and a string of all distinct characters needs n-1.

Remember one sentence: minimum insertions equals n minus the longest palindromic subsequence, because every unmatched character needs exactly one mirror partner inserted.
